claims.claim: Nursing clinical judgment is the observed outcome of critical thinking and decision-making: an iterative process that uses nursing knowledge to observe and assess presenting situations, identify a prioritized client concern, and generate the best possible evidence-based solutions (NCSBN working definition, 2019).
Clinical judgment is the thought process that allows nurses to arrive at a conclusion, based on objective and subjective information about a patient, to achieve positive patient outcomes.

Clinical judgment is commonly described as a four-phase process — notice, interpret, respond, reflect — a model associated with nursing scholar Christine Tanner and documented in NCSBN's review of the clinical judgment literature.

NCSBN developed the Clinical Judgment Measurement Model as a framework for valid measurement of clinical judgment, drawing on nursing, pedagogy, cognitive psychology, assessment, and decision-science literature, with input from more than 100 nursing experts and data from more than 200,000 NCLEX candidates.
Layer 3 of the CJMM names six directly measurable cognitive skills: recognize cues, analyze cues, prioritize hypotheses, generate solutions, take action, evaluate outcomes.
The CJMM is the basis for the case-based Next Generation NCLEX (NGN) items used in nursing licensure exams.
Clinical judgment is a learned skill developed through nursing knowledge, experience, and deliberate practice rather than an inborn trait.

Critical thinking, clinical reasoning, and clinical judgment are related but distinct: critical thinking is the broader reasoning skill set, clinical reasoning is the process of working through a situation, and clinical judgment is the resulting decision or outcome.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is clinical judgment a process or an outcome?
positions: NCSBN's 2019 guide defines nursing clinical judgment as 'the observed outcome of critical thinking and decision-making.'
OpenStax and much of the nursing literature describe clinical judgment as the thought process itself that leads to a conclusion.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents clinical judgment as the thinking nurses do to make care decisions (process framing) while noting NCSBN's outcome framing with attribution; both framings are cited so the distinction is transparent rather than smoothed over.

conflictingEvidence.issue: NCSBN pages returned 404 live on 2026-08-22; only Wayback Machine captures were readable.
positions: Canonical ncsbn.org URLs registered per registry rules.
Read copies are Internet Archive captures dated 2023-01-27 (CJMM page) and 2022-11-09 / 2022-12-19 (the two PDFs).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Canonical URLs recorded in sourceRecords with the exact Wayback capture noted in each record's notes; the content is stable standards-body material and the facts were cross-checked against OpenStax Fundamentals of Nursing 43.1.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft's framing of clinical judgment as an inborn personality trait or pure intuition was not supported by the verified sources and was replaced with the learned-skill framing.
The draft's claim that the four phases are 'assess, diagnose, plan, evaluate' (a confusion with the nursing process) was corrected to notice, interpret, respond, reflect.
correctionsNeeded: Used the verified NCSBN working definition with attribution instead of the draft's unverified paraphrase.
Added the six CJMM layer-3 cognitive skills from the verified sources.
Replaced the draft's intuition framing with the supported position that judgment is learned through knowledge, experience, and practice.
Clarified that cognition theory belongs to psychology, keeping the lesson focused on the practical nursing process.
rightsIssues: NCSBN materials are copyrighted with no explicit open license; used REFERENCE_ONLY with one short attributed quotation (the working definition) and synthesized facts throughout.
OpenStax Fundamentals of Nursing is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 with the book footer noting no LLM ingestion without OpenStax permission; used REFERENCE_ONLY with facts synthesized and no source prose adapted.
